title: Creek Critters: Parent Guide
endLine: Tiny creek animals share a food web and signal water health.

scenes.tts: What lives under a rock in a shallow creek? Lift one, and tiny animals scramble into view. You and your child will look closely, sort what you find, and check a guess together.
scenes.caption: What lives under a rock in a shallow creek? Lift one, and tiny animals scramble into view. You and your child will look closely, sort what you find, and check a guess together.
scenes.visual: Friendly schematic cutaway of a sunlit shallow park creek riffle filling most of the frame, with clear rippling water flowing gently over fist-sized rounded rocks and a shaded mossy bank on the right. Slow ambient ripples drift across the surface. One central rock tilts upward to reveal tiny stylized insect silhouettes darting off its underside. Title banner 'Creek Critters' fades in briefly at top left for two seconds, then clears.
scenes.narration: What lives under a rock in a shallow creek? Lift one, and tiny animals scramble into view. You and your child will look closely, sort what you find, and check a guess together.

scenes.tts: You do not need a science background to lead this trip. Your child practices slowing down, looking closely at tiny clues, and sorting what they find. They also practice making a guess and checking it against real evidence.
scenes.caption: You do not need a science background to lead this trip. Your child practices slowing down, looking closely at tiny clues, and sorting what they find. They also practice making a guess and checking it against real evidence.
scenes.visual: Same creek-and-bank scene, camera panning slightly right onto the shaded bank where a white plastic tray and a simple sketched notebook page appear. Three crisp, large callout icons appear one by one beside the tray (each under five words, high contrast): a hand lens labeled 'Look closely', three small sorting cups labeled 'Sort what you find', and a sketched question-mark-to-check arrow labeled 'Guess, then check'. Gentle creek ripples continue on the left.

scenes.tts: Pack a kitchen strainer, a white plastic tray, a plastic spoon, and closed-toe water shoes. Bring soap, clean water, sunscreen, insect repellent, and a clear plastic cup. Choose a shallow, slow riffle in a public park where collecting is allowed. Check posted water advisories. Go when water is low and clear, at least three days after heavy rain.

scenes.visual: On the shaded bank of the same creek scene, clean schematic drawings of the gear settle into place as named: kitchen strainer, white plastic tray, plastic spoon, clear plastic cup, pair of closed-toe water shoes, and a soap-and-water jug with sunscreen and repellent. Then the view shifts left to highlight the shallow, gently rippling riffle over fist-sized rocks; a simple calendar icon shows three sunny days after a raincloud, labeled 'Low and clear'.

scenes.tts: Stay within arm’s reach in or beside the water. Children under five stay on the bank with a second adult. Wade only in slow, clear water up to your child’s ankles. Wear closed-toe shoes for slippery rocks and hidden glass. Never drink creek water or taste wild plants, berries, or mushrooms. Keep tiny animals and small objects away from children under four. Call nine one one if choking.

Brief clear red-slash warning badges appear beside a muddy fast-water swirl, a tiny glass glint on the creek bed, and a wild berry plant on the bank, while an arrow shows the white tray tipping empty back at the water's edge.

scenes.tts: Fill the shaded tray with two to three centimeters of creek water. Ask your child, "What do you think lives under this rock?" Look for snakes before reaching. Lift the rock yourself and check underneath. Gently put the rock back if you see a crayfish, hellgrammite, or another animal that can pinch, bite, or sting. At a safe rock, have your wading child hold the strainer flat just downstream. Then gently rub the underside for about thirty seconds.

scenes.visual: Show the shaded white tray holding a shallow layer of creek water. Put the parent’s question in a speech bubble. In the riffle cutaway, show the adult looking before reaching, then lifting a small rock to check its underside. Show a crayfish beneath one rock and the adult settling that rock back gently. Show the adult choosing another small rock and checking it before rubbing. The child holds the strainer flat on the creek bed just downstream, within the adult’s reach.

scenes.tts: Tip the strainer into the white tray. Try three or four rocks, then give the mud a minute to settle. Watch for specks that crawl or dart. Ask, "Why do you think they hide under rocks?" Use the spoon, never fingers, to sort crawlers, swimmers, and animals that stay still.

scenes.visual: Top-down schematic view of the white tray resting on the bank beside the rippling creek. The strainer tips dark specks into the tray; a brief swirl of silt settles clear, and six stylized tiny critters begin moving in distinct paths. A speech bubble reads: 'Why do you think they hide under rocks?' A plastic spoon gently nudges critters into three sorted groups in the white tray labeled 'Crawlers', 'Swimmers', and 'Stay still'.

scenes.tts: You have sorted the animals by how they move. Now look at which kinds you found. If your tray held several kinds of mayfly and stonefly young, what might that suggest about the water?
scenes.caption: You have sorted the animals by how they move. Now look at which kinds you found. If your tray held several kinds of mayfly and stonefly young, what might that suggest about the water?
scenes.visual: Keep the tray large in frame with the creek edge visible. Show several schematic types of young mayflies and stoneflies, with distinct body shapes. Hold a high-contrast question above the tray: 'What might this mix suggest?'

scenes.visual: Hold on the same tray and question, 'What might this mix suggest?', for four and a half seconds. Keep the creek rippling softly while the viewer thinks.

scenes.tts: Several kinds can be a good sign. Most stonefly young and many mayfly young need cool, clean water with plenty of oxygen. Mayfly young usually have three tails and side gills. Stonefly young have two tails. Caddisfly young often live in sand or stick cases. Mostly worms, leeches, or tiny red larvae may suggest less healthy water.

scenes.visual: Keep the tray on screen. Show a mayfly young labeled 'Usually three tails' and point separately to its side gills. Show a stonefly young labeled 'Two tails'. Show a caddisfly young in a case with the label 'Often sand or sticks'. Briefly show a worm, a leech, and a tiny red larva beside the label 'Look at the mix'.

scenes.tts: A creek is a connected food web, and its hidden animals give clues to water health. Ask, "What do you think this one eats, and what might eat it?" Many eat leaf bits, and fish eat them. One visit is a clue, not a final answer.

scenes.visual: Pull back to the creek cutaway. Draw an arrow from fallen leaf bits to a group of unnamed small creek animals. Draw another arrow from those animals to a fish. Briefly show 'What eats what?' Keep the creek water moving.

scenes.tts: Pour the tray back slowly at the water’s edge near the rocks you sampled. Set each rock back as it was. Empty any containers before leaving. Wash hands with soap and water, wash the gear, and check everyone for ticks. The mix you found gives you a clue about the creek.

scenes.visual: The white tray tilts gently at the creek edge as the tiny critters swim safely back toward the riffle, and the lifted rock settles back onto the creek bed. On the bank, simple clean icons show soapy water rinsing hands and a small tick-check magnifying glass. The camera pulls back slightly as the sunlit creek flows calmly over the rocks, the food-web arrows glowing softly once more beneath the surface.
